teacher_glossary.definition: A visual or structural format used to organise and display data — including tables, graphs, models and mathematical relationships. At Year 9, the emphasis is on selecting the most appropriate representation for a given data type and investigation question, not just constructing any representation.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students default to a single graph type (typically bar graph) regardless of data type — they do not select a representation based on the nature of the data or the question being answered. The selection is habitual, not reasoned.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: An inappropriate representation obscures rather than reveals patterns. A bar graph used for continuous trend data hides the trend; a line graph used for categorical data implies a false continuum. If selection is not deliberate, the representation undermines the analysis it is supposed to support.
teacher_glossary.response: Model the selection decision explicitly: 'What type of data is this — continuous or categorical? What question am I answering — trend, comparison or relationship? Which representation makes the answer visible?' Present the same data in two representations and ask which reveals the pattern more clearly.

sub_terms.definition: The numerical range and increment chosen for a graph axis. Scale decisions include starting value, increment size, and whether the scale is uniform (equal increments throughout). Scale choices determine whether patterns are visible, exaggerated or hidden.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students select non-uniform scales, omit breaks when not starting at zero, or compress data into unreadable ranges — patterns become invisible or the visual impression is misleading.
sub_terms.response: Before students draw any graph, require them to determine the scale first: 'What is your minimum value? Maximum? What increment makes the data readable?' Review the scale before plotting begins.

sub_terms.definition: A graph that shows how a variable changes in response to a continuous independent variable, with data points connected by lines to show the trend. Appropriate when the independent variable is continuous (e.g. time, temperature) and the question is about a trend or rate of change.

A graph that compares values across discrete categories using separate bars. Appropriate when the independent variable is categorical (e.g. different materials, different species) and the question is about comparison rather than trend.

A graph that plots individual data points to show the relationship between two continuous variables, without connecting the points. Appropriate when investigating whether and how two variables are related — the pattern of scatter reveals the type and strength of the relationship.

An organised arrangement of raw data in rows and columns with headers and units. Tables display exact values and are the primary format for recording data during an investigation — they precede graphical representation.
The horizontal axis of a graph, typically representing the independent variable.
The vertical axis of a graph, typically representing the dependent variable.

A variable that can take any value within a range and is measured on a scale — such as temperature, time, mass or concentration. Continuous data is represented with line graphs or scatter plots because the values between measured points are meaningful.

A variable that falls into distinct groups or categories — such as species, material type or treatment condition. Categorical data is represented with bar graphs because there are no meaningful values between categories.

teacher_glossary.definition: Summary measures that describe key features of a data set — at Year 9, the core measures are mean, median and range. Selecting the appropriate descriptive statistic depends on the distribution of the data and what aspect of it needs to be communicated. The choice of statistic affects what the data appears to say.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students apply mean by default to all data sets without considering whether it is appropriate — they do not recognise that mean can be misleading for skewed data or data with outliers.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If mean is the only summary measure students use, they will produce misleading summaries of skewed data sets — the mean of a data set with extreme outliers does not represent the typical value. Statistical choice affects the validity of claims made from the data.
teacher_glossary.response: Present a data set with an outlier (e.g. test scores: 65, 68, 70, 72, 95). Calculate both mean and median. Ask: 'Which better represents the typical score? Why?' Repeat with a symmetrical data set where mean and median agree — the contrast builds selection judgement.

teacher_glossary.definition: The arithmetic average of a data set, calculated by summing all values and dividing by the number of values. Mean is the most commonly used measure of central tendency but is sensitive to extreme values — a single outlier can shift the mean significantly away from the typical value.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students calculate the mean correctly but use it uncritically for all data — including skewed data where the mean is pulled away from the centre by extreme values. They treat mean as the only way to summarise data.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If the mean is always used, summaries of skewed data will be misleading — students' conclusions will not represent the typical value in the data set, and claims based on the mean will overstate or understate the central tendency.
teacher_glossary.response: Present data sets where mean and median differ substantially and ask: 'If you had to describe the typical value, which measure would you choose? Why?' The comparison forces the student to evaluate rather than default.

teacher_glossary.definition: The middle value when a data set is arranged in order. Median is not affected by extreme values and is the preferred measure of central tendency for skewed data or data sets containing outliers. If the data set has an even number of values, the median is the mean of the two middle values.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students do not know when to prefer median over mean — they either never use median or use it only when told to, without understanding that skewed data or outliers make median more representative than mean.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Without median as a tool, students have no way to produce a representative summary of skewed data. They are limited to mean, which misrepresents the data in precisely the cases where summary statistics matter most.
teacher_glossary.response: Present a real-world context where median matters (e.g. household income data where a few very high incomes skew the mean). Ask students to calculate both and explain which better represents 'typical' — the real-world context makes the choice meaningful.

teacher_glossary.definition: The difference between the highest and lowest values in a data set, indicating the spread of the data. Range provides information about variability that central tendency measures (mean, median) do not — a data set can have the same mean but very different ranges, indicating different levels of consistency.
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students report the highest and lowest values rather than calculating the difference, or they do not recognise that range provides information about consistency and variability that mean and median cannot.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: Without range, students have no measure of how spread out their data is — they cannot distinguish between a reliable data set (small range) and an unreliable one (large range) when both have similar means.
teacher_glossary.response: Present two data sets with the same mean but very different ranges. Ask: 'Which set would you trust more? Why?' The comparison makes range's function as a reliability indicator concrete.

teacher_glossary.definition: A formula, ratio or proportional expression applied to process raw data into meaningful scientific information. At Year 9, this includes applying given formulae to calculate derived quantities, using ratios to express proportional relationships, and constructing representations where numerical accuracy is required (e.g. scaled Sankey diagrams).
teacher_glossary.failure_mode: Students can substitute values into a formula but cannot explain what the processed result represents — the mathematical step is mechanical rather than connected to scientific meaning.
teacher_glossary.why_it_matters: If mathematical processing is disconnected from scientific meaning, students produce correct numbers they cannot interpret. The calculation is not the end point — understanding what the result reveals about the phenomenon is the purpose of mathematical processing in science.
teacher_glossary.response: After every calculation, ask: 'What does this number tell you about the science? How does the processed result differ from the raw data, and why is the processed version more useful?' The interpretation question follows every mathematical step.

sub_terms.definition: A flow diagram where arrow width is proportional to the quantity being represented — typically used to show energy transfer and transformation, with wider arrows representing larger quantities. Constructing an accurate Sankey diagram requires applying ratios to determine arrow widths.
sub_terms.failure_mode: Students draw Sankey diagram arrows at arbitrary widths rather than scaling them proportionally to the quantities — the diagram becomes a sketch rather than a quantitative representation.
sub_terms.response: Provide the quantitative data and require students to calculate arrow widths as proportions of the total before drawing. Compare a correctly scaled diagram with an unscaled sketch and ask which provides useful information.

sub_terms.definition: A comparison of two quantities expressed as a proportion. In data processing, ratios are used to calculate relative values (e.g. percentage efficiency, proportional representation in diagrams).

A mathematical expression that defines a relationship between variables, used to process raw data into derived quantities (e.g. speed = distance ÷ time, efficiency = useful energy ÷ total energy × 100).
A data distribution with two distinct peaks rather than one. Mean and median can both misrepresent bimodal data by falling between the two peaks where few actual data points exist.

student_glossary.definition: A way of displaying data — like a table, graph or diagram — that helps you see patterns and answer questions. At Year 9, you need to choose the right type of representation for your data, not just use any graph.
student_glossary.example: If you're comparing the heights of different plant species, a bar graph works. If you're tracking how one plant grew over time, a line graph is better. Choosing the wrong one hides the pattern.

sub_terms.definition: The numbers and spacing you choose for your graph axes. A good scale makes patterns visible; a bad one hides them or makes them look misleading.
sub_terms.example: If your data ranges from 20 to 30, starting your y-axis at 0 wastes space and compresses the data. Starting at 18 spreads it out — but you must indicate the break.

sub_terms.definition: A graph showing how something changes as a continuous variable increases — data points are connected to show the trend.
sub_terms.example: Use a line graph to show how temperature changed over time during a heating experiment.

sub_terms.definition: A graph comparing values across separate categories using bars that don't touch.
sub_terms.example: Use a bar graph to compare the average height of different plant species — each species is a separate category.

sub_terms.definition: A graph showing individual data points for two variables, without connecting them — used to see whether and how the variables are related.
sub_terms.example: Plotting each student's study hours against their test score as a scatter plot lets you see whether more study is associated with higher scores.

sub_terms.definition: An organised grid of data with labelled columns and units — where you record your raw measurements.
sub_terms.example: Before you make any graph, your data should be in a table with clear headings like 'Temperature (°C)' and 'Time (s).'

sub_terms.definition: The horizontal (bottom) axis — usually shows the independent variable (what you changed).
The vertical (side) axis — usually shows the dependent variable (what you measured).
A variable measured on a scale where values between your measurements are meaningful — like temperature, time or mass. Use line graphs or scatter plots for continuous data.
sub_terms.example: Temperature is continuous — 25.5°C is a real value between 25°C and 26°C. That's why you connect the dots on a line graph.

sub_terms.definition: A variable that falls into separate groups with nothing meaningful in between — like types of material, species or colours. Use bar graphs for categorical data.
sub_terms.example: If you're comparing the strength of wood, steel and plastic, those are categories — there's no material 'between' wood and steel, so a bar graph is right.

student_glossary.definition: Numbers that summarise your data set — at Year 9, the key ones are mean (average), median (middle value) and range (spread). Choosing the right statistic matters because different ones can tell different stories about the same data.
student_glossary.example: For the data set 2, 3, 3, 4, 20: the mean is 6.4 but the median is 3. The mean is dragged up by that one high value — the median better represents the typical value here.

student_glossary.definition: The average — add up all values and divide by how many there are. It is the most common summary but can be misleading if your data has extreme values that pull the average away from the centre.
student_glossary.example: Five students scored 65, 70, 72, 68 and 95 on a test. The mean is 74, but most students scored around 68–72. The one high score pulls the mean up.

student_glossary.definition: The middle value when you put all your data in order. Unlike mean, median isn't affected by extreme values — it stays near the centre of the data even if one value is very high or low.
student_glossary.example: For scores 65, 68, 70, 72, 95 — the median is 70 (the middle value). That's closer to what most students actually scored than the mean of 74.

student_glossary.definition: The difference between the highest and lowest values — it tells you how spread out your data is. Two data sets can have the same average but very different ranges.
student_glossary.example: Data set A: 48, 50, 52 (range = 4). Data set B: 30, 50, 70 (range = 40). Both have a mean of 50, but set A is much more consistent.

student_glossary.definition: A formula or ratio you apply to your raw data to work out something new. The formula turns measurements into meaningful scientific information — like calculating efficiency from energy input and output values.
student_glossary.example: You measured that a motor used 100 J of energy and produced 75 J of useful work. Applying the efficiency formula (75 ÷ 100 × 100 = 75%) turns raw measurements into a meaningful result.

sub_terms.definition: A flow diagram where the width of each arrow is proportional to the quantity it represents — commonly used to show energy transfers where wider arrows mean more energy.
sub_terms.example: In a Sankey diagram for a light bulb, the input arrow (100 J) splits into a thinner useful light arrow (10 J) and a wider waste heat arrow (90 J) — the widths show you most energy becomes heat.

sub_terms.definition: A comparison of two quantities showing their relative size — like '3 out of 4' or '75%.'
sub_terms.example: If 30 out of 40 seeds germinated, the ratio is 30:40 or 3:4, which is 75% germination.

sub_terms.definition: A mathematical expression that shows how quantities are related, like speed = distance ÷ time.
sub_terms.example: Using the formula speed = distance ÷ time, if a ball rolled 2 metres in 0.5 seconds, its speed was 4 m/s.

sub_terms.definition: Data that has two peaks instead of one — the average falls between the peaks where few actual values are, making it misleading.
sub_terms.example: If half the class scored around 50% and half scored around 80%, the mean of 65% doesn't represent anyone — the data is bimodal.
